7de82f9956:
Once the always-on memory of chapter 08 is in place, there are three more ways to steer Claude Code. This chapter covers reusable prompts and skills that load on demand (3.2), the choice between thinking first and editing at once (3.4), and the techniques that turn a first attempt into a correct one (3.5).

Along the way you'll see what a command or skill physically is, who receives it, and how its frontmatter changes what the model sees and may do. You'll see why a forked skill and the Explore subagent keep your context clean, and what plan mode blocks and what approving a plan changes. And you'll see why a test, an example or an interview works better than "no, not like that". Java/Spring examples run throughout.
db0fa31734: Reading time: 3 to 3.5 hours  ·  Companion code, 19 Python examples and 1 Java program for this chapter: ccarf-companion/09-commands-skills-plan-mode/ (run bash run_all.sh; everything works offline, the "model" is a scripted fake, and the simulators use only the standard library)
06374f448e: Product details change quickly. Everything about Claude Code in this chapter was checked against the public documentation in October 2026. Where a detail wasn't stated precisely, or differs between versions, the text says check the docs. The exam tests concepts that have stayed stable across versions. Don't memorise option spellings from a chapter.
eaf4b7ed3d:
Anything you would type twice belongs in a file, and where the file lives decides who gets it: a command or skill under the repository's .claude/ reaches every teammate who pulls, one under ~/.claude/ reaches only you, and either one costs almost nothing until it is invoked, which is why procedures go there and universal conventions go in CLAUDE.md.

Before Claude edits anything that is large, multi-file, architectural or unfamiliar, make it read and propose first (plan mode, with the Explore subagent absorbing the noisy search); and when its first result is not right, correct it with signals it can check (two or three concrete input/output examples, a test suite, a short interview that surfaces the decisions you have not made), bundling problems that interact into one message and fixing independent ones one at a time.
16ba3816c2:
Both halves are the same idea seen from two sides: context is the scarce resource, and every technique in this chapter decides what enters it, when, and in what form.

A skill stays out of context until it's needed. A forked skill and the Explore subagent do their reading somewhere you can throw away. Plan mode moves the expensive mistake (a wrong design) to the cheapest moment (before any file has changed). Examples and tests replace vague adjectives with something the model can compare its output against.

Hold on to that, and the details below stop being a list of features. They become consequences.
ded1e5625a:
The official task statements list the following.

Task 3.2:

  • the difference between project-scoped .claude/commands/ (shared via version control) and user-scoped ~/.claude/commands/ (personal);
  • skills in .claude/skills/ with SKILL.md files and their frontmatter, including context: fork, allowed-tools and argument-hint;
  • context: fork running a skill in an isolated sub-agent context, so verbose output doesn't pollute the main conversation;
  • personal skill variants in ~/.claude/skills/ that don't affect teammates;
  • the choice between skills (on-demand, task-specific) and CLAUDE.md (always loaded, universal).

Task 3.4:

  • plan mode for complex, large-scale, multi-file or architectural changes, and for choices between several valid approaches;
  • direct execution for simple, well-scoped changes;
  • plan mode for safe exploration before committing;
  • the Explore subagent for verbose discovery that would otherwise exhaust the context;
  • plan mode for investigation combined with direct execution for implementation.

Task 3.5:

  • two or three concrete input/output examples when prose is interpreted inconsistently;
  • test-driven iteration: tests first, then share failures to guide improvement;
  • the interview pattern, to surface considerations the developer hasn't anticipated;
  • interacting problems in one message, independent problems sequentially.

Sections 04 to 13 teach each 3.2 bullet explicitly, sections 14 to 19 each 3.4 bullet, and sections 20 to 27 each 3.5 bullet. The summary table at the end restates them one by one.
402563658e: None of this was invented for language models. Each mechanism is an old software-engineering answer to a problem that comes back whenever a new tool gets capable enough to be dangerous, or repetitive enough to be tedious. Knowing the lineage tells you what the design is for. And that tells you which exam option is the sensible one.
b766e891ed:
The first answer to "I type this a lot" was the shell alias in the 1970s and 1980s, and then the Makefile target. Both have the property that matters here: they're named, versioned text that expands into a longer action.

The personal version (~/.bashrc) is yours. The project version (Makefile, later package.json scripts, ./gradlew tasks) is committed, so every contributor runs the same release target. Spring teams know the split well. ~/.m2/settings.xml and ~/.gradle/init.d/ are personal; pom.xml and build.gradle are shared.

A Claude Code slash command is the same two-level arrangement, for prompts instead of build steps.
07e2bc2ec0:
When chat assistants arrived, people kept their best prompts in text files and snippet managers and pasted them into a box. The weakness was the same as copying a build script into a wiki: no single source of truth, no review, no distribution.

Claude Code's custom slash commands made the prompt a repository artifact. A command is a Markdown file whose name becomes the command. It goes through the usual code review, and a new hire gets the team's /review on the first git clone.
85abc4bae4:
A prompt is one instruction. Real procedures need reference tables, templates and helper scripts. They also need a way for the assistant to know when to use them, without a person having to remember.

Anthropic introduced Agent Skills in late 2025 as a general format: a folder with a SKILL.md, where only a short description is always visible and the rest loads when relevant. The design principle is progressive disclosure, borrowed from good documentation and from lazy initialisation in software. Pay for detail only when someone asks.

Claude Code adopted the format. Its current documentation treats a file in .claude/commands/ and a skill as two ways to create the same /name. Commands kept working, and skills add supporting files, invocation control and automatic loading. The exam guide still describes commands and skills as two things. So this chapter teaches both, and flags where the current docs have merged them.
3922926243:
Wherever mistakes are expensive, industry has separated "decide" from "do". Architecture review boards approve a design before the build starts. terraform plan shows the change set before apply. Flyway and Liquibase can validate or render a migration before running it. Databases have EXPLAIN.

The common structure is a read-only pass that produces an artifact a human can cheaply approve or reject, followed by a mutating pass.

The same instinct shows up in the language-model literature as Plan-and-Solve prompting (2023), which asks the model to devise a plan before solving. In coding assistants it appears as architect-then-editor modes (for example in Aider, 2024). Claude Code's plan mode turns the instinct into an enforced permission state. While it's on, the tools that change files aren't available until you approve.
1507b8fc3a:
Three much older practices explain the three techniques of 3.5.

Kent Beck's test-driven development (popularised around 2002) made a failing test the specification and a passing test the definition of done. A coding agent that can run tests is the same loop with a different typist.

Few-shot prompting came out of GPT-3 (2020). For many tasks, a handful of worked examples in the prompt beat a paragraph of description, because examples are concrete where prose is ambiguous.

Then there's requirements elicitation, as old as the profession: the analyst interviews the stakeholder before anyone writes code. If you've been burned by a spec that missed the one rule the business assumed everyone knew, you'll recognise the interview pattern at once.

Papers such as Self-Refine and Reflexion (both 2023) studied models improving their own output from feedback. The practical lesson matches the engineering one. Feedback that is specific and checkable works. Feedback that is a mood doesn't.
31fd2ef848:
Start with a fact that explains most of Claude Code's design. The context window is finite, everything in it is read on every request, and model performance degrades as it fills. Anthropic's own best-practices page opens with this constraint.

A session shows it in three ways:

  • Tokens cost money and latency, because the whole history is resent each turn (chapter 01 measured the quadratic growth).
  • Attention isn't uniform. A rule buried in a 900-line file is followed less reliably than the same rule in a 60-line file (chapter 08).
  • Clutter has a half-life. A failed approach, a 20,000-token grep result or a pasted stack trace stays in the window. It keeps influencing later turns until the session is cleared.
84b9176716:
Chapter 08 covered the part of Claude Code's knowledge that is always loaded: CLAUDE.md files and unscoped rules. They're the right home for things that apply to nearly every task, and the wrong home for everything else.

Consider a release checklist of 120 lines that two people run twice a month. In CLAUDE.md, it's read, billed and diluted on every request from every developer. That includes the 99 percent of requests that have nothing to do with releases. Sixty such procedures would make the memory file unusable.

The cost isn't only tokens. The one rule that matters ("never edit application-prod.yml") now competes for attention with fifty-nine irrelevant checklists.
306ec688d1:
The Spring analogy is lazy initialisation. CLAUDE.md is application.yml, read at startup by every bean. A skill is a @Lazy bean, registered by name and instantiated only when something asks for it. The registry entry (its description) is cheap. The object (its body) isn't.

As with @Lazy, the trade-off is that something must decide to ask. For a command, a person decides by typing /name. For a skill, the model decides by reading the one-line description, or a person decides by typing the name. So the most important sentence in any skill is its description, and section 07 is devoted to it.
acb7110c73:
One more design consequence is worth stating early, because the exam probes it. Loading on demand is not enforcement.

A skill that says "never edit the production config" is read only when invoked. Even then, it's guidance the model weighs. Things that must hold in every session, whatever the model decides, belong in hooks and permission rules (chapter 03 and chapter 08), not in a better-worded skill. Section 10 gives the full decision table.
498671a98e:
The first thing 3.2 asks is a placement question: which directory does this file go in? The answer is the same rule chapter 08 used for CLAUDE.md. The directory decides the audience.

Everything under the repository's .claude/ is committed. It reaches every teammate on their next pull, and every CI job that checks the repo out. Everything under ~/.claude/ lives in your home directory. It applies to you in every project, and to nobody else.
8bd69c10dd:
The exam turns this into scenario questions in both directions.

The forward case: a team wants a /review command that every developer has as soon as they clone or pull. The answer is .claude/commands/ inside the project. Putting it in ~/.claude/commands/ makes it work for its author and nobody else. That's the most common mistake in real teams too ("it works on my machine", for prompts). Putting the checklist in CLAUDE.md loads it on every request, and it can't be invoked by name.

The reverse case: a developer wants the team's commit-message skill to also add a Jira key in her personal style. Editing the committed .claude/skills/commit-message/SKILL.md changes the behaviour for the whole team on the next pull. The correct move is a personal skill variant in ~/.claude/skills/ under a different name (my-commit-message). Teammates are unaffected, and there's no collision to reason about.
806546b9cc:
In current Claude Code documentation, a file at .claude/commands/deploy.md and a skill at .claude/skills/deploy/SKILL.md both create /deploy. Existing command files keep working. Command files accept the same frontmatter as skills, except name and paths. A command in a subdirectory gets a colon namespace: .claude/commands/frontend/component.md becomes /frontend:component.

A skill is the richer form. It lives in a directory, so it can bundle reference files and scripts. And it supports automatic loading when its description matches the task.

When two entries share a name, the docs give this order:

  • enterprise beats personal;
  • personal beats project;
  • a skill beats a command file of the same name;
  • plugin skills are namespaced, so they never collide;
  • a nested skill is addressed with its path (/apps/web:deploy) and doesn't replace the root one.

The page doesn't say what happens between a personal command and a project skill of the same name. Check the docs, and avoid the situation by choosing distinct names.
f10dca9c41:
Two operational facts matter in practice.

First, Claude Code watches the skills directories. Adding or editing a skill takes effect in the current session without a restart. The exception is a top-level skills directory that didn't exist at startup. That needs a reload command (/reload-skills in the docs read for this chapter).

Second, nested skill directories load lazily. apps/web/.claude/skills doesn't appear in the / menu until Claude has read or edited a file in apps/web. Say a developer starts at the repository root, looks for the web deploy skill, and doesn't find it. She hasn't made a mistake. It's the same lazy behaviour chapter 08 showed for subdirectory CLAUDE.md files.
45e825ec78:
A command is a Markdown file. The file name without .md is the command name, and subdirectories become colon namespaces. Everything after the optional frontmatter is the prompt Claude receives when you type /name.

That's all a command is: a saved prompt with a name. Its power comes from three things you can put around the prompt text: frontmatter, argument placeholders, and embedded shell output.
6b744230c6:
Typing /review develop substitutes develop for $0 and sends the result as your message.

Because the file is committed, the checklist gets reviewed in a pull request like any other change. When someone sharpens rule 2, it improves for everyone. A review prompt typed fresh by twelve developers drifts into twelve review prompts.
6e5b06e512:
Argument syntax is where real commands break, so it pays to be exact. The docs read for this chapter define:

  • $ARGUMENTS: the whole string typed after the command;
  • $ARGUMENTS[N] and $N: positional arguments, zero-based;
  • named placeholders ($from, $to), declared with an arguments frontmatter field;
  • quoting for multi-word values (/my-skill "hello world" second);
  • a literal dollar sign, written as \$.

Three behaviours at the edges decide whether a command degrades gracefully. If the body contains no placeholder at all, Claude Code appends the line ARGUMENTS: <value>, so the text isn't lost. An indexed placeholder with no matching argument stays literally as $1 in the prompt, and Claude may treat it as a real value. A named placeholder with no match becomes an empty string.

Substituted values are inserted literally and not re-expanded.
63ad248aeb:
Older command documentation used $1 as the first argument. The skills page read for this chapter says positional arguments are zero-based. Both facts are real, from different times. Which one your installed version follows is a "check the docs" item.

The safe choices are the ones that don't depend on it: use $ARGUMENTS for free-form input, or declare named arguments. Example 04 runs ten cases of the substitution rules, including the one-based legacy mode.
1dd9b422bf:
Write the argument-hint to match what the body consumes. And say in the body what to do when an argument is missing.

The hint ([base-branch], <module-path>) shows up in autocomplete. It's documentation, not validation. Nothing stops a developer from typing the command bare. A skill that needs a module name and has only a hint will, when invoked bare, either guess or scan everything. The safer form puts the rule in the prompt: "If no module is given, ask which module; do not scan the whole repository."
457d370a33:
A command or skill can embed the output of a shell command with the !`command` form, which must start a line or follow whitespace. The command runs before Claude sees the prompt, and its output replaces the placeholder.

This is the right tool for facts that change every time: the diff, the log since the last tag, the list of failing tests. Claude starts the turn already holding them, instead of spending a tool call to fetch them.

Three documented rules govern it:

  • The command is permission-checked like any other. So it must be pre-approved with allowed-tools; otherwise, outside auto mode, the invocation aborts.
  • A failing command aborts the whole invocation. That means a non-zero exit, with a carve-out for search and comparison commands that use exit 1. Claude never sees a half-filled prompt.
  • A policy setting can disable shell injection entirely. Then the placeholder is replaced by a notice.

The fixture command release-notes.md deliberately has no allowed-tools. So example 05 first shows the abort. Then it shows the same command succeeding once Bash(git log *) is pre-approved, and aborting again when the tag doesn't exist.
a4f07f9544: The Java/Spring equivalent of the idea is a Gradle task that depends on gitLog and feeds its output to renderReleaseNotes. The injected shell command is the dependency that runs first. The prompt is the task that consumes it. As in a build, a failed dependency stops the chain.
e0ebf35b1f:
A skill is a directory. SKILL.md is the only required file. Everything else is optional, and exists to keep SKILL.md short. The directory name is the default skill name and the default /name.

The file opens with YAML frontmatter between two --- lines, followed by the instructions. The frontmatter must start on the very first line of the file. Put a blank line before it, and the frontmatter isn't read.
eac7771c77:
Notice four design choices.

  • The description names both what the skill does and the words a developer uses when they need it ("consumer", "listener", "event handler"). That sentence is how the model finds it.
  • The body refers to bundled files through ${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}, so it works wherever the skill is installed.
  • It says what to do when an argument is missing.
  • It's short, because the conventions live in a reference file that's read only if the task reaches that step.
89d4467860:
The skills page lists the fields below. All are optional, and only description is recommended. The exam names three: context: fork, allowed-tools and argument-hint.

A senior reader should know the rest exist. Real skills use them. And several of the exam's distractors are fields with plausible-sounding names that don't exist.
00d4d45abc:
Two properties of the frontmatter parser cause more lost afternoons than any single field.

Unknown fields are silently ignored. So allowed_tools (underscore), argument_hint or context: forked produce no error and no effect. The skill runs inline, with default permissions, and nobody notices until the verbose output arrives.

And booleans are forgiving. They accept true/false, yes/no, on/off, 1/0, in any letter case. That's convenient. It also means a typo'd value silently falls back to the default.

The cheap defence is a linter in CI. The companion's skillsim.py contains a small one, and example 03 runs it on six deliberately broken files and on every fixture. Recent versions of Claude Code also offer claude plugin validate <dir> for skill directories (check the docs).
a9e9a7251a:
A skill that's never found costs nothing and does nothing.

The model decides whether to load a skill by comparing the user's task with each skill's listed description. It's the same way it decides whether to call a tool, by reading the tool's description (chapter 05). So the description isn't documentation for humans. It's the routing rule.

"Utility for code stuff" can't be matched to anything. Compare "Audit a Maven or Gradle module for vulnerable, outdated or duplicated dependencies. Use when asked about CVEs, dependency updates, version conflicts, or before a release". It names the artefact, the verbs and the situations, in the words a developer would actually type.

Example 07 makes the point with a deliberately naive word-overlap matcher (a toy, not how Claude chooses). Three vague descriptions match none of three realistic tasks. Three precise ones match all three.
e978f31ec0:
The docs add two mechanical limits that turn this from style advice into engineering.

First, each entry's description plus when_to_use is cut at 1,536 characters in the listing. So the key use case must come first. A trigger phrase placed after the cap doesn't exist for the model. Example 07 proves it with a skill whose only trigger sits at character 2,100.

Second, the listing as a whole has a character budget that scales with the context window. The docs say 1 percent of it; whether that's counted in characters or tokens is a "check the docs" item. When there are too many skills, Claude Code keeps every skill name but drops descriptions, starting with the skills you invoke least.

Forty skills with 400-character descriptions will lose descriptions. Trim them, use name-only overrides for the rest, or raise the budget setting. /doctor and /context show what the listing costs.
cd2e2c35f4:
An explicit invocation (/dependency-audit order-service) is a deliberate act, with the arguments typed. A model invocation is Claude noticing that the task matches a description and loading the skill itself, with arguments inferred from the conversation.

Each has a failure mode. The people who'd benefit from explicit commands forget them. Model invocation fires too rarely when the description is vague, and too often when it's broad. For "triggers too often", the docs' troubleshooting advice is to make the description more specific, or to set disable-model-invocation: true and make it manual.

Anything that deploys, publishes, deletes or spends money should be manual by default. "The model decided it was appropriate" isn't an approval process.
a515ea2a64:
Much exam-prep material describes allowed-tools as a way to restrict the tools a skill may use. The current documentation is more precise, and the difference is the kind that separates a safe design from an unsafe one.

allowed-tools pre-approves the listed tools during the turn that invokes the skill: they run without a permission prompt. It does not restrict the other tools, which keep following your normal permission mode and rules (they ask, as usual). The pre-approval clears when you send your next message.

If you want a skill to be unable to edit files, there are three mechanisms:

  • a read-only agent (agent: Explore on a forked skill);
  • disallowed-tools, which removes tools from the pool while the skill is active;
  • a deny rule in settings, which wins over everything.
105b90a474:
Example 08 runs these four cases on the permission simulator. With allowed-tools: Read Grep Glob active, an Edit still comes back as "ask", not "blocked". After the next user message, even the pre-approval is gone. And a deny rule plus disallowed-tools produce "deny" and "unavailable".

For the exam, hold two readings at once. If a question says a skill "restricts tools to read-only" using allowed-tools, that's the common framing, and the answer it expects is probably the allowlist. If a question asks what actually guarantees a skill can't modify files, the strong answers are the read-only subagent, disallowed-tools, or a deny rule.

When the two conflict, read what the option claims it guarantees. Mark the finer points as "check the docs" for your version.
97d7d178f9:
That file is the pattern for side-effecting skills: manual only, one pre-approved script with a pattern for its arguments, and a refusal rule for bad input.

The refusal rule is guidance. If prod must be unreachable from a developer laptop, put a deny rule or a hook in front of ./scripts/deploy.sh prod.
d41276e0e6: Having fifty skills installed should cost almost nothing, and the loading design makes that true. There are three levels. The level a piece of text sits at decides when you pay for it.
298b8a1b34:
Three consequences follow, and all three are testable.

First, invocation is sticky. Once the body is in the conversation, it stays across turns; it isn't re-read from disk. So a skill that said "run the tests" won't notice if you edit the file mid-session. If the rendered content is identical on a second invocation, Claude Code adds a short "already loaded" note instead of a second copy.

Second, compaction keeps only the start. When the context is compacted, each skill's most recent invocation is re-attached, but only its first 5,000 tokens. All re-attached skills share a 25,000-token budget, filled from the most recent. Instructions at the bottom of a long skill can fall off. Put the rules that matter most at the top. If a skill seems to stop being followed late in a long session, invoke it again.

Third, a skill is advisory. The docs' troubleshooting for "Claude stops following a skill" says two things. A rule that must hold every time should move into a hook (a skill can carry its own hook in its hooks frontmatter). And guidance meant for the whole task should be worded that way: "run the tests after every edit", not "run the tests".
db7e2fb52b:
The docs' 500-line guidance ("keep SKILL.md under 500 lines and move reference material to supporting files") is the practical rule that makes level 3 real.

The mistake to avoid is a 900-line SKILL.md. It behaves like a CLAUDE.md that happens to load later. Then it sits in the conversation and gets truncated at compaction.

Split it instead. Put a short procedure in the body, tables and templates in reference/, and anything computable in scripts/. A script that parses 3,000 lines of mvn dependency:tree and prints 25 rows costs 25 rows of tokens.
294e503f3c:
Take the dependency audit. Suppose you want to answer "which modules use a vulnerable Jackson version?" in a 40-module Maven build. The work is: find every pom.xml, read each, compare versions, maybe read the BOM. That's hundreds of kilobytes of intermediate material for one 20-row answer.

Run it inline, and all of that intermediate material lands in your main conversation. It sits there. It's resent on every later turn. And it pushes the decisions you made an hour ago toward the edge of the window.

Nothing was wrong with the audit. It was just the wrong place to do it.
9a3ca4185d:
context: fork solves this by running the skill in a subagent: a separate conversation with its own fresh context window. The skill's body becomes the subagent's task prompt. The subagent does the noisy work, and its result is what returns to the main conversation.

The subagent doesn't see your conversation history. The main conversation never sees the 40 file reads. When the subagent finishes, its context is discarded.
c72b1c3664:
Read the last two lines of that file as part of the mechanism, not as polish. What returns to the main conversation is whatever the subagent says last. So the skill must bound the return: a table of at most twenty rows and a one-line count. A forked skill that ends with "report your findings" can return as many tokens as it read.

The agent field chooses the subagent type:

  • Explore is the built-in read-only searcher (next sections);
  • Plan is the read-only research agent used during plan mode;
  • general-purpose is the default, and it can act;
  • or you name a custom agent from .claude/agents/.

Choosing Explore here does two jobs at once. It's fast at searching. And Write and Edit are denied, so the agent type enforces "do not edit any file" instead of prose merely requesting it.
2f8b61f456:
Two related mechanisms point in opposite directions, and confusing them is a favourite trick.

A forked skill selects a subagent to run the skill. A subagent definition can instead preload skills through a skills field in its own frontmatter, injecting their full content at startup. The first is "run this skill over there". The second is "give this subagent these skills". A skill with disable-model-invocation: true can't be preloaded.

The pages read for this chapter didn't settle two details: whether a forked skill's subagent loads the project CLAUDE.md files, and how its result is attributed. Check the docs before relying on either.
b34b7a3379:
Chapter 02 covered subagents as an orchestration pattern. There, the coordinator's job is to give each subagent a complete task, because subagents don't inherit context.

The same rule applies here in miniature: the skill body is the subagent's entire briefing. If it says "audit the module we were just talking about", the fork will audit nothing.
9039690295:
The exam phrases 3.2's last decision as "skills for on-demand, task-specific workflows; CLAUDE.md for always-loaded, universal standards". The test that decides it is frequency of relevance.

If a rule applies to nearly every edit ("Java 21, constructor injection, no Lombok"), it belongs in CLAUDE.md. Or in a path-scoped rule, if it applies to a kind of file (chapter 08). If it's a procedure for a specific task ("how to cut a release", "how to add a Kafka consumer with a DLQ"), it belongs in a skill or command. A 200-line release procedure in CLAUDE.md is the textbook anti-pattern.

The table puts every mechanism in this part of the guide next to its siblings.
afb05a786d:
Candidates tend to miss the bottom row of the table: everything except hooks and permission rules is guidance.

Skills and commands are higher-fidelity than CLAUDE.md, because they're read at the moment they matter. But they're still prompts that the model weighs against everything else in the context. If the requirement is "must always" or "must never", the answer is a hook or a deny rule.

A skill can carry a hook in its frontmatter. That's the pattern for "this rule only matters when this skill is running".
1927791731: The fixture repository in the companion folder is a small order platform with the artefacts this chapter has discussed. Read its layout once. It shows how a team splits the work.
3a39052cc6:
Count what each artefact costs and who gets it.

  • CLAUDE.md stays at five lines, so every request pays almost nothing.
  • /review and /release-notes are manual prompts: zero cost until typed.
  • dep-audit costs a 190-character listing line. When used, it costs a fork that reads dozens of files in a throwaway context.
  • new-kafka-consumer costs a listing line. It loads its body (and, if the body asks, its two bundled files) only when someone adds a consumer.
  • deploy is invisible to the model's autonomous routing.

Alex's personal artefacts exist on Alex's machine. Bea has an empty home directory, and she sees exactly the project-scoped set (example 01 asserts this).
6a00451a11:
Projects loaded by the Claude Agent SDK can use the same skills, as long as the agent loads project settings and the skill tool is allowed. The sketch below runs the audit headlessly, the way a CI job in chapter 10 would.

Option names follow the SDK at the time of writing. Check the Agent SDK skills page for the current spelling; this is exactly the kind of detail that changes.
ec511b80c4:
Two details are the point.

Without setting_sources=["project"], the SDK doesn't read the repository's .claude/ directory, and the skill simply isn't there. (Check the docs: the default has changed between SDK versions.)

And the skill is available to the agent as a tool, so allowed_tools must include it.

In CI, this is how the same team skill a developer invokes by hand becomes a pipeline step, with no second copy to maintain. Chapter 10 builds the surrounding job.
6c4451daf3:
Java/Spring teams sometimes ask for the equivalent in their own language. At the time of writing, there's no official Java Agent SDK that this chapter can verify.

So the usual pattern is to treat Claude Code as a build tool. A Gradle Exec task or a Maven exec-maven-plugin execution runs claude -p "/dep-audit services/orders" --output-format json. A later step parses the JSON result.

Chapter 10 covers the flags and the JSON contract. The point here is that a slash command or skill typed after -p is invoked like any prompt. (Check the docs for the exact behaviour of slash commands in non-interactive mode.)
6d53ca19e6: Each anti-pattern below is a real mistake that the exam turns into a wrong answer option. For the first two, the broken and fixed forms are shown as files.
e214b30a7a:
Project scope is version-controlled and arrives with the clone.

User scope (A) works for the author only and depends on manual copying, which drifts. CLAUDE.md (C) loads the checklist on every request, and it isn't invocable by name. A hook (D) is for deterministic enforcement on lifecycle events, not for a prompt a person chooses to run.

Example 01 shows a teammate with an empty home directory receiving /review from the project scope.
8042bf5780:
The symptom is context pollution. The intermediate output sits in the main window and is resent every turn. Forking moves the noisy work out and returns only the result.

max_tokens (A) limits output per response and does nothing for accumulated history. CLAUDE.md (B) would make it worse, loading the procedure on every request. Compacting after each run (D) treats the symptom. It costs a summarisation each time, and it can lose the decisions you wanted to keep.

Example 09 measures the difference: about 33,000 tokens against about 100 in the main history.
82d1b665bb:
A personal skill variant under a different name changes nothing for teammates, and there's no name collision to reason about.

Editing the committed skill (A) or the team CLAUDE.md (C) imposes her preference on everyone. D multiplies a personal preference across people, and it can't be enforced.

The fixture repository has this exact pair. Example 02 shows the personal skill listed only for its owner.
59e55c7412:
Study material often describes the field in restricting language. So in some questions, a plain "restrict tools" option may be the expected answer. But the current docs say pre-approval, and a question that asks what is guaranteed is asking about exactly this difference.

C and D invent behaviours. Example 08 runs an Edit under an active allowed-tools: Read Grep Glob, and it comes back as "ask". Check the docs for your version, and prefer a mechanism whose name says what it does.
7a5d755f25:
An agent that can edit files will start editing as soon as it has a plausible idea. For a one-line fix, that's exactly what you want. For "split the 1,800-line OrderService", it isn't, and the reasons are economic, not stylistic.

The first plausible idea is rarely the best one. The cost of discovering that grows with each file already touched. And reviewing forty edited files is far harder than reviewing a one-page plan.

A wrong design found in a plan costs a sentence of feedback. The same design found in a diff costs a revert, a re-read, and the lost context of the aborted attempt.
e6329ee9bc:
Plan mode separates exploration from commitment. It enforces the separation with permissions, not with a polite request.

In the docs' words, plan mode tells Claude to research and propose changes without making them. It reads files, runs exploratory shell commands, and writes a plan. It doesn't edit your source, and edits stay blocked until you approve the plan.

The software-architecture analogy is exact. You wouldn't let a team start coding a service decomposition before the design review. Plan mode is the design review, enforced by tool permissions instead of process discipline. And rejecting the result is free, because nothing in the working tree has changed.
2c9dc23b44:
There's a second, quieter benefit, which the official best-practices page states directly. Separating research from implementation avoids "solving the wrong problem".

An agent that jumps to code produces something that compiles and passes the tests it wrote for itself. And it answers a question you didn't ask. Reading first forces the model to say what it found, what it assumes, and what it won't touch. A reviewer can check those in two minutes.
d7c6996911:
Plan mode is one of the permission modes:

  • default (called Manual in the UI): asks before most actions;
  • acceptEdits: file edits and common filesystem commands run without asking;
  • plan;
  • auto: a classifier model reviews actions instead of you;
  • dontAsk: only pre-approved tools run;
  • bypassPermissions.

Each makes a different trade between convenience and oversight, and a session can move between them.
bae8c14221: Interactive: press Shift+Tab until the status bar shows plan mode on, or prefix a single prompt with /plan. Which modes Shift+Tab cycles through depends on your version and settings (check the docs).
4ca4712383: Non-interactively: combine --permission-mode plan with -p to get an analysis with no edits. This is a CI technique (chapter 10). The exact interaction between -p, plan mode and approvals is a check-the-docs item.
fa5f04bac5:
Claude reads files and searches. It asks you clarifying questions through the AskUserQuestion tool, which is also the engine of the interview pattern in 3.5. It delegates to read-only subagents, and it runs shell commands for exploration. Edit and Write are blocked.

What happens to a shell command depends on the session:

  • With bypass permissions available, neither the classifier nor a prompt applies to planning commands.
  • With auto mode available and the setting on (it is by default), the classifier reviews commands other than removals of critical paths.
  • Otherwise, commands outside the built-in read-only set prompt for approval.

For the exam, the practical summary is the first paragraph. For a safety review, it's the list: shell commands in plan mode are not uniformly read-only. Plan mode is a strong default, not a sandbox. If a plan session must be provably unable to change anything, combine it with deny rules or run it in a read-only checkout.
0819cdc8ac:
When the plan is ready, Claude presents it and asks how to proceed. The three options are the ones in the figure. The first reads differently when auto mode is unavailable ("Yes, auto-accept edits") or when the session started with bypass permissions.

A fourth option appears when the showClearContextOnPlanAccept setting is on. It approves the plan and clears the planning context, and it matters. A long exploration leaves a long context. Starting implementation with a clean window and only the plan is often better (section 18).

Pressing Ctrl+G opens the proposed plan in your editor, so you can change it before Claude proceeds. The mechanism that submits the plan is an exit-plan tool (named ExitPlanMode in the tools reference; check the docs).
767f46e0c9:
Everything here maps to ideas you already know. The plan is the artefact of a read-only pass, like a Terraform plan. The approval gate is the same gate a change-advisory board provides.

The difference is speed. The whole cycle of explore, propose, review and approve takes minutes. That makes it cheap enough for any task where your own next thought would be "wait, which approach?".
991ed12b78:
The official criteria are two lists.

Plan mode fits complex, large-scale changes, changes that touch many files, tasks with several valid approaches where the choice matters, and architectural decisions. The exam's sample for plan mode is restructuring a monolith into microservices.

Direct execution fits simple, well-scoped changes. Examples: adding a validation check to one function, or fixing a single-file bug with a clear stack trace.

The Anthropic best-practices page compresses this into one test worth memorising: if you could describe the diff in one sentence, skip the plan. Planning pays when you're uncertain about the approach, when the change modifies multiple files, or when you don't know the code being modified.
50fef606fb:
The mechanical-change row catches people who memorised "many files means plan". A rename across 40 call sites touches many files. But the diff is one sentence and the approach is unambiguous, so a plan adds a review gate with nothing to decide.

Conversely, adding caching to six files has a small file count and a large decision: Redis, Caffeine or none, and where to invalidate. That deserves a plan.

The criteria are about uncertainty and reversibility. File count is only a proxy.
dd5e4a6590:
Planning isn't free. It costs a turn or two. For a task that didn't need it, a plan is ceremony: the developer reads a plan that says what the prompt already said. The docs call plan mode "useful, but also adds overhead" and say to ask for small, clear-scope changes directly.

The failure on the other side hurts more. Go "direct" on a change with several valid approaches, and the model silently picks one, edits twelve files, and you discover the choice in code review.

A reasonable personal heuristic: if you're about to type "and make sure it also...", you're describing a plan. Use plan mode.
57b6730033:
Investigation is verbose. To find every caller of OrderService.placeOrder in a 600-file monolith, Claude runs dozens of greps and partial reads. If all of that lands in the main conversation, the plan gets written by a model whose context is mostly grep output. The decisions you've made so far are a small fraction of what it's reading.

The Explore subagent exists to absorb exactly this. It's a built-in read-only subagent specialised for file discovery and code search. Claude delegates a request to it, such as "map OrderService: public methods, callers, transaction boundaries, Kafka producers and consumers, tables touched". Explore does the searching in its own context window and returns a summary. Your main context keeps the summary.
df77c89719:
Here are the facts to retain, from the sub-agents page:

  • Explore and Plan are both read-only (Write and Edit denied).
  • Plan is the research agent used during plan mode.
  • The general-purpose agent can do both exploration and action.
  • Which model Explore runs on depends on provider and account. Check the docs, since the page lists several cases.

In current versions, subagents can spawn their own subagents, up to a configurable depth. For discovery you rarely want that.

A forked skill can also name the Explore agent directly (agent: Explore). That's how dep-audit is a read-only audit by construction. Or you can ask in plain language: "use a subagent to investigate how token refresh works, and whether we have OAuth utilities to reuse".
cd84404951:
This is the third appearance of one idea, and the exam treats the three as variants of each other. A forked skill moves noisy work out of the main context. The Explore subagent does the same for discovery. The Task tool in the Agent SDK (chapter 02) is the programmatic form.

In each case, the verbose part happens in a window you can throw away, and only a bounded result returns.

The cost is the same in each case too. The delegate doesn't see your conversation, so the request must be complete. And a summary can leave out something you'd have wanted. Mitigate that by specifying the return format ("file:line references and the transaction boundary for each caller").
1e3108dad2: When shouldn't you use it? For a question one Grep can answer, delegating costs more than it saves. Subagents add a round trip and a context to set up. The break-even is roughly "more reads than you'd want to see yourself".
6dc6302317:
The exam's preferred pattern is a sequence, not a choice. Use plan mode to investigate and agree an approach. Then use direct execution to implement it, in phases small enough to verify.

The best-practices page names four phases:

  1. explore: read, in plan mode;
  2. plan: ask for a detailed implementation plan and, if you wish, edit it with Ctrl+G;
  3. implement: leave plan mode and code against the plan, with tests;
  4. commit.

The sequence works because each phase has a different failure mode and a different cheapest fix. A misunderstanding is cheapest to fix in explore, a wrong design in plan, a bug in implement.
d49f9ab581:
Running the plan in a fresh session is the point of the dashed arrow in the figure. The docs' own clean-context option on plan approval exists for it.

After a long exploration, the window is full of file reads the implementation doesn't need. The plan is the distilled output of all that reading. Starting implementation with only the plan gives the model its full attention for the edits. It also gives you a written record of what was intended.

The cost is that anything in the exploration but not in the plan is gone. So a plan must state its assumptions, its files, its phases (each with a test gate), and what's out of scope. The "out of scope" line is what makes the drift check meaningful.
beedde6adb: The team repo is a Spring Boot 3 order platform for a telecom retailer. OrderService is 2,400 lines. It handles order capture, pricing, inventory reservation and fulfilment events. The goal is to extract fulfilment into its own service.
0e9ecee4ed:
Look at what the investigation surfaced. The shared transaction in placeOrder() would have broken a naive "move the methods and call over REST" implementation. Reading before anyone edited is what found it.

The task had two valid answers, so the plan presented both, with trade-offs and a recommendation. The phases give each execution step a test gate. And "start phase 1 only" turns a 20-file project into a first step small enough to verify with the existing suite.

This is the exam's "multiple valid approaches, architectural decisions, multi-file" case, in the shape it will take at work.
c9d99d8c43:
A few cross-references matter here.

Chapter 08's CLAUDE.md tells the planning session your conventions (constructor injection, ProblemDetail, the outbox pattern), so a good plan already follows them. The plan session reads the same memory the execution session will.

Chapter 04 covers task decomposition and session management: resuming, forking, starting fresh with a summary. That's the machinery behind the two-session pattern.

Chapter 10 runs the same flow unattended. A CI job can use plan mode with -p to produce an analysis. And a reviewer session should be different from the author's session, because a fresh context isn't biased toward code it just wrote.
a29fc1a7fe:
Large-scale, multi-file, architectural, multiple valid approaches: every signal points to plan mode.

Detailed instructions (A) can't replace discovering what the code actually contains, such as the shared transaction in the transcript. Switching late (C) means finding the complication after the first dozen edits. Relying on tests (D) assumes the existing tests cover cross-service behaviour that doesn't exist yet.

This is the official sample for 3.4.
1fe606829d:
The location is known, the cause is known, and the diff is one sentence. This is the typical shape of a direct-execution question.

A plan (A) restates the prompt. Repository-wide exploration (C) is scope creep, unless you want that audit separately. An interview (D) is for requirements you haven't decided, and here the requirement is stated.

Note that "with a failing test first" is a 3.5 technique inside a direct task.
1d7464b1a3:
The problem is verbose discovery exhausting the window. Explore reads in its own context and returns a summary, so the main session keeps room to plan.

Direct execution (A) removes the planning, not the exploration, and the task is architectural. Clearing (C) throws away the progress. Skimming (D) trades correctness for tokens on a security-critical migration.

The detail that earns marks is specifying the return format, so the summary is usable.
661e3d6e37:
The first result from a coding agent is rarely the last. That isn't a flaw. It's how a model works when the task is under-specified. Three separate things go wrong, and each of the 3.5 techniques addresses one.

Ambiguity. Your prose could be read several ways. The model picks one reading, and it isn't the one you meant. Examples fix that, because an input and an output can't be misread.

No feedback signal. The model stops when the work "looks done", because that's the only signal it has. So you become the verification loop. A test suite fixes that: it gives a pass or fail the model can read in the conversation.

Unstated decisions. There are choices you haven't made (rounding, who may trigger it, what happens on retry), and the model fills them in silently. An interview fixes that, because the model asks before it builds.
3326fe00d4:
A fourth failure comes from the way people react to the first three: correcting by adjective. "No, not like that". "More robust". "Cleaner". "Handle edge cases". An adjective asks the model to guess what you'd approve, and a guess has no way to converge. Every technique in this chapter replaces an adjective with something checkable: a concrete example, a failing test, an answered question.

There's a context cost too. Each failed correction leaves the failed attempt and the correction in the window, and both keep influencing later turns.

The best-practices page puts the rule plainly. If you've corrected Claude more than twice on the same issue in one session, the context is cluttered with failed approaches. Clear it, and start again with a more specific prompt that includes what you learned.
5df56efc99:
The usual exam shape for this technique is a code-migration task where prose instructions are interpreted inconsistently across files. The remedy is two or three concrete input/output examples that show the transformation.

Why it works is information-theoretic, and easy to demonstrate. A prose description defines a set of programs consistent with it, and the model samples from that set. Every concrete example removes the members that disagree with it. Three well-chosen examples can shrink the set to one. Three obvious ones may remove nothing.
262864a16d:
Example 15 makes this literal. The prose specification is "normalise phone numbers to E.164 for US customers".

The example generates 18 plausible implementations. They differ along three choices the prose leaves open:

  • whether an existing +44 number passes through unchanged;
  • what happens to an extension such as x22 (dropped, kept, or invalid);
  • what an invalid number returns (null, an empty string, an exception).

Then it adds examples one at a time and counts the survivors.
215e8cf544:
Read the table as a guide to what to put in the prompt. The first two inputs are the ones a person writes naturally, and they eliminate nothing. Every plausible implementation handles a US number with punctuation the same way. The examples that earn their place are the ambiguous cases: the extension, the foreign number, the invalid input.

Choose examples for the cases where a reasonable engineer could disagree, not for the cases everyone gets right.

Say what each example demonstrates ("extension is dropped", "invalid input returns null, never throws"). A labelled example is a rule with evidence. An unlabelled one is a puzzle.
0fb3a89fc2:
The fixed prompt contains the three cases that actually split the code base: instants, date-only values and local display. It states the "never rely on the JVM default zone" rule inside an example where it applies. And it gives the model a way out ("list it at the end") instead of forcing a guess.

Two to three is the right number for most transformations. One example invites copying its quirks. Many examples cost tokens and start to over-constrain.
21d971ea61: Examples have a second use, which connects to the next section: an input/output pair is also a test case. In a Java project, the examples in the prompt and the examples in the test suite can be literally the same table.
f415a95ac6:
Anthropic's best-practices page puts the single most useful sentence about agentic coding first: give Claude a way to verify its work.

Claude stops when the work looks done. Without a check it can run, "looks done" is the only signal available, and you become the verification loop. Give it something that returns pass or fail, and the loop closes on its own. Claude does the work, runs the check, reads the result, and iterates until the check passes.

The check can be anything that produces a signal readable in the conversation: a test suite, a build exit code, a linter, a script that diffs output against a fixture.
6f27e7886c:
Test-driven iteration is the disciplined form.

Write the tests first, or have Claude write them from your examples and review them. Confirm they fail for the right reason. Then ask Claude to make them pass.

Share the failures exactly as the runner prints them: the failing assertion, the expected and actual values, the stack trace. That text is far more specific than any description you'd write, and the model reads it well. Repeat.

The tests are the specification you can execute. Each round tells both of you how far apart the implementation and the specification still are.
1280703488:
A few practices make this work in a real repository.

  • Give the test command in the prompt or in CLAUDE.md, so the model doesn't guess it (chapter 08).
  • Prefer running a single test or class while iterating, and the full suite at the end. The best-practices page says the same.
  • Tell the model to address the root cause rather than suppress the error ("fix it and verify the build succeeds; do not just catch the exception"). A model asked only to make a check pass will sometimes weaken the check.
  • Review the tests, since they are the specification. A wrong expected value will be satisfied as faithfully as a right one.
  • Match the strength of the gate to the importance.

A prompt that says "run the tests and iterate" works in any session. For unattended runs, the docs describe stronger forms. One is a /goal condition, re-checked after every turn. Another is a Stop hook that runs the check as a script and blocks the turn from ending until it passes. (Check the docs for the current mechanics, including caps on consecutive blocks.)

A second opinion from a verification subagent helps when the model that wrote the code shouldn't be the one grading it.
03c78c78a2:
The Java/Spring reader already has this loop. It's red-green-refactor, with JUnit as the oracle and Claude as the typist.

What changes is the speed of the cycle, and the temptation to skip the red step. Skipping it ("write the code and the tests together") produces tests that were written to pass, and they verify nothing. Insist on seeing the failure first.
50a18b7fe0:
If the same test keeps failing after two corrections, the problem usually isn't the code. Either the test encodes a requirement the model can't infer, or the context is carrying a failed approach that keeps pulling it back.

The remedy in the docs is blunt and effective. Run /clear, then write one better prompt that includes what you learned: the failing test, the cause you now understand, and the example that disambiguates.

If you'd rather keep the session, rewind (Esc Esc or /rewind) restores the conversation, the code or both to an earlier checkpoint. Checkpoints cover Claude's file edits, not changes made through shell commands. They're no substitute for git.
ed311178c9:
Examples fix the ambiguity you can see, and tests fix verification. Neither helps with the decisions you haven't noticed you haven't made.

For a feature of any size, those are most of the risk. Can refunds be partial? How does rounding work? Who may trigger the endpoint? What goes into the audit log? How do retries behave? A one-shot prompt doesn't ask. The model fills each gap with a plausible default, and you discover the defaults in code review, if you're lucky.

The interview pattern reverses the flow. You give a minimal description and ask Claude to interview you, using the AskUserQuestion tool, about technical implementation, edge cases, concerns and trade-offs. It keeps going until the decisions are covered, then writes a specification. It's requirements elicitation, done by the assistant.
7ea2eaa4c2:
The pattern has four parts:

  • A minimal seed. The less you pre-decide, the more the interview surfaces.
  • An instruction not to ask obvious questions. That's what keeps it from asking "should the code compile?".
  • A stopping condition (until covered).
  • A written artefact (SPEC.md).

Once the spec exists, the recommended move is a fresh session to implement from it: clean context, with the spec as the brief. The most useful specs are self-contained. They name files and interfaces, state what's out of scope, and end with an end-to-end verification step.
2e5ced6b9a:
Example 17 plays both sides with scripted turns. The model asks six questions, one per hidden decision: idempotency, partial refunds, rounding, approval threshold, audit trail, and who can trigger it. The stakeholder answers each, and the resulting spec contains all six, with no "TBD".

As a one-shot, the same prompt would have made six silent guesses, and none would have been visible until review.

The check at the end of the example is one you can apply to a real spec. For every decision the business cares about, is there a sentence that settles it?
5095503ea4:
Where does the interview sit relative to plan mode? They're cousins. Plan mode answers "how will you change the code?" after reading the code. The interview answers "what should the code do?" before.

For a feature in unfamiliar territory, you can chain them. Interview to write the spec. Run plan mode against the spec and the code to produce the implementation plan. Then execute in phases.

Use the interview when you can't enumerate the requirements yourself. Skip it when you can (the null-check task in scenario 6). It's also the right answer when an exam question says the developer isn't sure about the design considerations in a domain. The model can surface considerations you haven't anticipated.
c0f0643e5b:
The last technique in 3.5 is a rule about batching. When several problems interact, meaning the fix for one changes what the correct fix for another is, put them in one message, together with the intended end state. When they're independent, fix them sequentially, one message each.

The reasoning follows from how the model works with partial information. Given one issue, it makes the most local assumption available. If the other issues change that assumption, each fix is correct in isolation and wrong together.
feb7fd33cc:
Example 18 shows both halves, with a tiny code base held in a dictionary.

Three issues interact: rename Order.phone to msisdn, make the validator check E.164 on the renamed field, and make the serializer emit the renamed field. Send them as three separate messages, and a patch agent that sees one issue at a time applies each fix with the name it knows. The validator still reads phone, and the integration check fails. Send them as one message with the end state, and the agent updates all three consistently. The check passes.

Two genuinely independent issues (return 201 on create; fix a typo in a log message) give the same result in either order. Separate messages keep each one small, focused and individually verifiable.
fc9c2362a6:
A useful way to apply the rule is to draw the dependency between issues. If fixing A could change what B should be, or if A and B edit the same lines or the same contract, bundle them. If you can fix and verify A without knowing anything about B, separate them.

Separation also helps your own review, since each change is a coherent diff with its own test.
6394aee89e:
The techniques so far prevent drift. This section is about recovering from it, because the exam's refinement questions often take the form "the first result is wrong, what next?". The tools are small, and worth knowing precisely.

  • Esc stops Claude mid-action with the context intact, so you can redirect.
  • Esc twice, or /rewind, opens the rewind menu. From there you can restore the conversation, the code or both to an earlier checkpoint, or summarise from a chosen message.
  • "Undo that" asks Claude to revert its own edits.
  • /clear resets the context between unrelated tasks.

Course-correct early. The best results come from tight feedback loops. A correction at step 2 is cheap. The same correction at step 20 means undoing everything built on the mistake.
5ada3d8f1c:
The inconsistency comes from ambiguity in prose, and examples remove ambiguity.

"Consistently" (A) is an adjective with no content. Majority voting (C) pays five times to sample the same ambiguous distribution. A larger model (D) may read more carefully, but it still has to guess what you meant.

Example 15 shows that three well-chosen examples reduce 18 candidate behaviours to one, while two obvious ones remove none.
fda8392d2b:
Test-driven iteration gives a signal the model can read, and the rounding rule becomes executable.

More prose (A) is still prose. Self-review (C) in the same context is weak, because the reviewer shares the author's assumptions (see chapter 10 on separate sessions). D abandons the task.

Example 16 shows the shape: a real runner, real failure text, four rounds to green.
d389f208e0:
The missing business rules are decisions nobody had made explicit.

Plan mode (A) plans the code from the prompt as given. If the rule isn't in the prompt, it isn't in the plan. A longer prompt (C) is limited by what she can think of, and that's the problem. D finds the rules in production.

The interview surfaces considerations she hasn't anticipated, and the spec turns them into a reviewable artefact. Example 17: six questions, six resolved decisions.
d4dffe23bd:
The rule is to bundle interacting problems and separate independent ones. The rename, validator and serializer interact. The status code and the typo interact with nothing.

One message for all (A) clutters the context and mixes the review. Three strict sequential messages (B) split the rename from its consumers, which is the failure in example 18. D drops requirements.
ce8f41896e:
Each stage addresses a different uncertainty: requirements (interview), design in unfamiliar code (Explore plus plan), and correctness (tests per phase).

Direct execution (A) pays for a wrong design in code. Plan mode alone (C) assumes the requirements are in the prompt. Five implementations (D) multiply the review work without resolving either uncertainty.
706bfbba3e: Use the companion folder ccarf-companion/09-commands-skills-plan-mode/. Everything runs offline with Python 3, plus a JDK 17 or later for the Java program. Parts A to C use the simulators. Part D uses a real Claude Code installation, if you have one.
0ade089e21: Scope. Run python3 01_scope_who_sees_what.py. Add a command file to fixtures/home_bea/.claude/commands/, and predict what changes for each developer before you rerun it. Then move review.md from the repo to Alex's home and rerun. Who loses /review?
d93557a6cc: Fork. In 09_context_fork.py, change the number of build files from 40 to 10, then to 200. At what size does the fork stop being worth the loss of context, in your judgement? Write down the rule you'd give your team.
70cb3222a5: Plan. Add three of your own tasks to 12_plan_vs_direct_triage.py: one you're sure is direct, one plan, and one you're unsure about. Disagree with the function on at least one, and change a rule so it agrees with you. What did you have to add?
bdbc80378b: Examples. In 15_io_examples_narrow_the_spec.py, add a fourth dimension (e.g. whether a trailing "#" is stripped), and see how many examples you now need. State the general rule.
a4daf76def: Real session (optional). Use a scratch repository with Claude Code installed. Create the /review command and the dep-audit skill. Run /context before and after invoking the skill, both inline (remove context: fork) and forked. Then start with claude --permission-mode plan and ask for a plan for a three-file change. Note every difference from the simulators.
9215b61a64:
Done when:

  • you can say, without notes, where a command, a skill, a rule and a hook each belong, and why;
  • you've seen a misspelt frontmatter field do nothing;
  • you can explain, in two sentences each, why allowed-tools isn't a sandbox, why a forked skill needs a bounded return, and why a plan needs an out-of-scope line;
  • you can choose between an example, a test and an interview for a given first result that's wrong.
